newsitem.title: MONTSERRAT: Death toll feared at 20 from Montserrat volcano.
newsitem.headline: Death toll feared at 20 from Montserrat volcano.

text.p: Montserrat officials said on Monday they feared that as many as 20 people had been killed last week when a rumbling volcano rained superheated rocks and gas on the island.
"It could be as high as 20 (dead)," said Claude Hogan, a spokesman for the British territory's government.

He spoke as new flows of extremely hot rocks and gases from the Soufriere Hills volcano, located in the southern part of the island, set more houses on fire. Deadly pyroclastic flows -- fast-moving bursts of 930-degree Fahrenheit (500-degree Celsius) volcanic material -- devastated seven villages in southern Montserrat last Wednesday.

Hogan said nine or 10 bodies had been recovered and officials were fairly confident that another 10 people had been killed, but their bodies not yet found, in the village of Farm's, which was burned almost to the ground in the disaster.
"That village we know is all but consumed except for a few houses on the steeper side of the valley. The village is gone. Those 10 people were in there, we know," he said.
He said another 24 people were still considered missing.

On Monday rock and ash surged down the volcano's southwestern flanks at mid-afternoon, sending a dark cloud into the sky that obliterated the sun, and roaring through evacuated villages near Plymouth, Montserrat's capital. There were no reports of additional injuries.

Baroness Liz Symons, British undersecretary of state with responsibility for the Caribbean, visited Montserrat on Sunday and Monday and reiterated her government's commitment to giving financial support to the tiny island and to developing its northern third, which is considered safe.

People caught by last week's eruption had disregarded scientists' warnings to stay out of the danger zone, some having refused orders to leave, others visiting regularly to feed animals and tend their property. An evacuation order for the area has been in effect for 14 months.
The danger zone was expanded late last week, forcing another 1,500 people to crowd the eastern Caribbean island's "safe" section.

Some residents also were taking advantage of the inauguration of ferry service on Sunday to travel to the nearby island of Antigua to make air connections, as Montserrat's only airport, located in the expanded danger zone, was closed on Wednesday and was expected to remain so indefinitely.
Five people were burned so badly that they were flown to nearby islands for treatment. Among them was a young girl from Nebraska, identified as Mary Gloupeck, who had suffered a badly burned hand.
Hogan said the danger zone was considered fully evacuated. Island police had removed residents from three southern villages by force on Sunday, the Caribbean News Agency reported.
Montserrat Chief Minister Bertrand Osborne said he has no plans for an off-island evacuation.

Last week's deaths were the first in Montserrat blamed on the volcano since it roared to life on July 18, 1995, after nearly four centuries of virtual dormancy. The island's population has dropped by a third to 6,800 since the volcano awoke.
